Bringing your own data

Source: vignettes/data-prep.Rmd
data-prep.Rmd

Every spax model needs three inputs that line up: demand (the people who may use a service, counted where they live), supply (what each facility offers) and the travel time between them. This guide answers one question: how do I get my own data into that shape? It prepares the inputs with prep_data() and works through three problems you are likely to meet: facility IDs that must match, travel times that are unknown, and demand that comes as area totals rather than a grid. It ends with the inputs of the allocation model, including observed counts in a long table. The examples use the Cornwall GP data, described in The Cornwall GP example data. The spax() interface and the allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

The guide uses spax with terra for the grids, sf for the small areas and dplyr for tables.

library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

The inputs

prep_data() takes two shapes of input. The first sections use rasters: a demand grid, a stack of travel layers and a table of facilities, as for the FCA indices. The last two use vectors and a travel matrix named by ID, as for the allocation model. The code reads the population grid, the stack of travel times and the table of all practices, the Isles of Scilly included.

# Residents per grid cell (WorldPop 2020)
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
# Travel minutes, one layer per practice
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
# Practices as a plain table
gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)

c(practices = nrow(gp), travel_layers = nlyr(travel_grid))
    practices travel_layers 
           55            55 
head(names(travel_grid))
[1] "L82001" "L82003" "L82004" "L82006" "L82007" "L82008"

Each travel layer is named with the practice’s NHS code, the same code as in gp$practice. That shared code is what lines the inputs up.

Match facilities by ID, not by order

prep_data() takes the table of practices with two more arguments: id_col names the column of facility IDs and supply_cols the column of supply. spax then matches each row of the table to the travel layer with the same ID. To see this, the code computes an accessibility index from the table in its own order and in reverse order. The index is an enhanced two-step floating catchment area index (E2SFCA, one of the FCA indices): GP full-time equivalents (FTE) per resident, with nearer practices counting more. Its weights fall with travel time on a Gaussian curve, and the travel scale σ, which sets how fast they fall, is 10 minutes, as in Getting started.

e2sfca <- spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10))

# The practices in their own order, and in reverse order
in_order <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
reversed <- prep_data(pop, arrange(gp, desc(practice)), travel_grid,
                      id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

index_in_order <- spax(in_order, e2sfca)
index_reversed <- spax(reversed, e2sfca)
all.equal(values(index_in_order$accessibility), values(index_reversed$accessibility))
[1] TRUE

spax() returns the index as a raster in the result’s accessibility element, in GP FTE per resident. The two indices are equal: the row order of the table does not matter. A named supply vector is matched by name in the same way. An unnamed vector or a matrix is used in layer order, and then keeping the order right is your job.

A facility that is in one input and not the other stops with an error. Here the table drops the Scilly practice while the travel stack keeps its layer:

prep_data(pop, filter(gp, !scilly), travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
 [1m [33mError [39m in `prep_data()`: [22m
 [33m! [39m Length of travel layers (55) must match length of facilities (54)

The error compares counts: 55 travel layers against 54 practices. To keep only some facilities, select their layers by ID, travel_grid[[ids]], as the grid recipe in the next section does with [[gp$practice]]. A code in the table that matches no layer, such as a typing error, passes prep_data() but stops with an error when spax() runs the model.

Decide what unknown travel means

For an FCA index, an unknown (NA) travel time means no access: the pair is left out of the sums. Decide whether that is true for your gaps before you compute an index. In the Cornwall travel grid, NA marks cells with no residents, pairs with no road connection and journeys over 180 minutes. Here the gaps come from the Isles of Scilly: their practice cannot be reached by road from the mainland, mainland practices cannot be reached from the islands, and some cells on the smaller islands reach no practice at all. The code counts the populated cells with unknown travel in each practice’s layer, then the residents of the cells with a road route to each side.

# Count the populated cells with unknown travel in each practice's layer
populated <- !is.na(pop)
missing_cells <- global(is.na(travel_grid) & populated, "sum")[[1]]
table(scilly_practice = gp$scilly, missing_cells)
               missing_cells
scilly_practice 73 6963
          FALSE 54    0
          TRUE   0    1
# Cells with a road route to the Scilly practice (L82017) or to the
# mainland (here the first layer, a mainland practice)
road_scilly <- !is.na(values(travel_grid[["L82017"]], mat = FALSE))
road_mainland <- !is.na(values(travel_grid[[1]], mat = FALSE))

# Residents in each group
residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
by_route <- round(c(
  to_mainland = sum(residents[road_mainland]),
  to_scilly_practice = sum(residents[road_scilly]),
  no_road_link = sum(residents[!road_mainland & !road_scilly], na.rm = TRUE)
))
by_route
       to_mainland to_scilly_practice       no_road_link 
            541184               1206                277

Each mainland layer has 73 populated cells with unknown travel, all on the islands, and the Scilly layer has 6,963, every mainland cell among them. Of the residents, 541,184 live in cells with a road route to the mainland practices, 1,206 in cells that reach the Scilly practice and 277 in cells that reach neither.

The index above used all 55 practices. The code compares its median in the two groups of cells, per 1,000 residents.

# Index per 1,000 residents with all practices
with_scilly <- 1000 * values(index_in_order$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
scilly_medians <- round(c(
  mainland_median = median(with_scilly[road_mainland]),
  scilly_median = median(with_scilly[road_scilly])
), 2)
scilly_medians
mainland_median   scilly_median 
           0.49            7.59

The islands become a separate system with one practice and few residents, so their median index is 7.59 GP FTE per 1,000 residents against 0.49 on the mainland. The cells that reach no practice get no index (NA), and their residents drop out of every practice’s demand.

The islands do have access, by boat and air, which the road-based travel times do not represent. So the guides model mainland Cornwall only, with the grid recipe from The Cornwall GP example data. The last line looks for populated cells with an unknown travel time.

gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

# Any populated cell with an unknown travel time?
anyNA(values(travel_grid)[!is.na(values(pop)), ])
[1] FALSE

FALSE: every populated cell of the mainland grid has a travel time to every mainland practice. The Cornwall GP example data explains each line of the recipe. For the allocation model, prep_data() asks you to choose what unknown travel means, as Inputs for the allocation model shows below.

Turn area totals into a demand grid

Demand often comes as totals for administrative areas, while an index on a grid needs a count of people per cell. cornwall_lsoa holds ONS mid-2024 population estimates for 336 mainland small areas (LSOAs). Spreading each total evenly over its cells would ignore where people live inside the area, so the WorldPop grid serves as a pattern: transform_pmf() turns it into shares that sum to 1, and transform_demand() rescales those shares so that each area keeps its own total. The code spreads the totals of the small areas.

# Mainland small areas as a terra vector in the grid's coordinates
lsoa <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  vect()

# The WorldPop grid as shares that sum to 1
pattern <- transform_pmf(pop)

# Spread each area's total over its cells
# (density = TRUE returns people per cell; FALSE returns shares)
lsoa_grid <- transform_demand(x = lsoa, value_col = "pop", pmf = pattern, density = TRUE)
Warning: 40 area(s) cover no grid cell or have zero weight; their counts are
dropped and the surface is rescaled. Use larger areas or a finer template.

The grid cells are about 1 km across, and many town LSOAs are smaller. An area whose polygon contains no cell center cannot receive its count. The function drops those areas and rescales the grid to the overall total, so their residents would land in other areas’ cells. The fix is larger areas or a finer grid. Here the code merges the LSOAs into their middle-layer areas (MSOAs): an LSOA name ends in a letter, and dropping it gives the MSOA name (Cornwall 013A is in Cornwall 013).

# Merge LSOAs into MSOAs, adding up their counts
# (terra names the summed columns sum_pop, sum_pop_65p, ...)
lsoa$msoa <- sub("[A-Z]$", "", lsoa$name)
msoa <- aggregate(lsoa, by = "msoa", fun = "sum")

# Spread each MSOA total over its cells with the WorldPop pattern
ons <- transform_demand(
  x = msoa,
  value_col = "sum_pop",
  pmf = pattern,
  density = TRUE,
  full_output = TRUE  # also return the area totals
)

c(
  areas = nrow(msoa),
  ons_total = sum(msoa$sum_pop),
  grid_total = round(global(ons$surface, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]])
)
     areas  ons_total grid_total 
        73     583289     583289 
# Largest difference between an area's total and its grid total
largest_gap <- max(abs(ons$totals$original - ons$totals$redistributed))
signif(largest_gap, 2)
[1] 0.00069

All 73 areas keep their totals: the largest difference is a tiny fraction of a person. The new grid has the ONS counts with the WorldPop pattern inside each area. The two sources differ in date and method, so their ratio varies by area. The code summarizes the median ratio per area and maps the ratio per cell, with the color scale capped at 0.5 and 1.5.

# ONS count over WorldPop count in each cell, and its median per area
ratio <- crop(ons$surface / pop, msoa)
ratio_by_area <- extract(ratio, msoa, fun = median, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
round(summary(ratio_by_area), 2)
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.74    1.00    1.07    1.15    1.18    3.73 
plot(
  clamp(ratio, 0.5, 1.5),
  axes = FALSE,
  range = c(0.5, 1.5),
  col = hcl.colors(50, "Blue-Red 3"),
  main = "ONS mid-2024 / WorldPop 2020 residents per cell"
)
lines(msoa, lwd = 0.3, col = "grey40")

Within an area both grids follow the WorldPop pattern, so each area has nearly one color: the ratio of its two totals. In 55 of the 73 areas the ONS estimate is higher (the median ratio is 1.07), and in one it is 3.7 times the WorldPop count. Choose the source that matches your question, say which you used, and keep to it within one analysis. The other guides use the WorldPop grid directly.

If your raster is a density, people per square kilometer, multiply it by terra::cellSize(x, unit = "km") first: longitude-latitude cells are not all the same size.

Spread a rate rather than a count

rasterize_demand() does a different job: it reweights a pattern by an area rate, such as the share of residents aged 65 and over, and returns shares of one total rather than counts that keep each area’s total. The code builds the older population on the grid this way and measures how much of each area’s known count it keeps.

# Share of residents aged 65 and over in each MSOA
msoa$share_65 <- msoa$sum_pop_65p / msoa$sum_pop

# Reweight the WorldPop pattern by that share: the result is shares
older <- rasterize_demand(
  x = msoa,
  value_col = "share_65",
  prior = pattern
)
older_counts <- older * sum(msoa$sum_pop_65p)

# Each area's grid total as a fraction of its known count
kept <- extract(older_counts, msoa, fun = sum, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2] /
  msoa$sum_pop_65p
round(quantile(kept, c(0, 0.5, 1)), 2)
  0%  50% 100% 
0.29 1.01 1.46

The shape is plausible: population times the local share aged 65 and over. Area totals are not kept, though: the areas end up with between 0.29 and 1.46 times their known count. To place the older residents themselves, spread their counts: transform_demand(x = msoa, value_col = "sum_pop_65p", pmf = pattern, density = TRUE) keeps every area’s total. Use rasterize_demand() when only the shape matters, such as a relative weight per cell.

Inputs for the allocation model

The allocation model, a conditional logit model (CLM, the standard model of a choice among several options), gives each small area’s residents a probability of registering at each practice, or with the outside option: a practice outside the data. It takes numeric inputs named by ID: demand by small area, supply by practice and a matrix of travel minutes between them, here cornwall_travel. The code prepares every small area and practice, the Isles of Scilly included.

# Every small area and practice, the Isles of Scilly included
all_areas <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_lsoa)
all_gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
all_demand <- setNames(all_areas$registered, all_areas$lsoa)
all_supply <- setNames(all_gp$gp_fte_extg, all_gp$practice)

prep_data(all_demand, all_supply, cornwall_travel)
 [1m [33mError [39m in `prep_data()`: [22m
 [33m! [39m active travel is missing; declare missing_travel = 'omit' to leave out unknown pairs

Here an origin is a small area, where people live, and an active origin is one with demand above zero. Unknown travel from an active origin is an error unless you say what it means. There are three ways to say it. missing_travel = "omit" leaves the unknown pairs out of the model, as the FCA indices do, and records that it did. A travel time of Inf declares a pair known to have no link. That is a known value, so prep_data() accepts it. Or you drop the rows and columns with unknown times. The code shows the first two.

# Leave the unknown pairs out, and record that policy
prep_data(all_demand, all_supply, cornwall_travel, missing_travel = "omit")
<spax data> 337 origins (337 active) x 55 facilities
  demand      606,796
  travel      unknown for 337 active origins
  policies    missing demand: error; missing travel: omit
# Declare the unknown pairs known to have no link
no_link <- replace(cornwall_travel, is.na(cornwall_travel), Inf)
prep_data(all_demand, all_supply, no_link)
<spax data> 337 origins (337 active) x 55 facilities
  demand      606,796
  travel      unknown for 0 active origins
  policies    missing demand: error; missing travel: error

The first print records that every area has an unknown time (each mainland area to the Scilly practice, and the Scilly area to the mainland practices) and the policy that left them out. The second records none. In the allocation model both give the pair no weight, so a model gives the same results with either. They differ in what the data records: an unknown time for omit, a known absence for Inf.

The guides drop the islands instead, as for the grid, with the small-area recipe from The Cornwall GP example data. Its last line, obs_flows(), comes in the next section:

areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
d
<spax data> 336 origins (336 active) x 54 facilities
  demand      604,471 registered residents (July 2026)
  supply      GP FTE excluding GPs in training (June 2026)
  travel      minutes; unknown for 0 active origins
  policies    missing demand: error; missing travel: error

prep_data() lines up demand, supply and travel by their names, so their order does not matter, and a supply name that matches no travel column stops with an error. No area is left with an unknown travel time. The labels in metadata stay with the data and with every result. spax does not convert units.

Observed counts in a long table

Observed counts usually arrive as a long table, one row per origin and facility. cornwall_flows has one row per small area and practice with at least one registration. obs_flows() says which column holds the origin IDs, which the facility IDs and which the counts. A pair missing from the table counts as 0, and duplicate pairs are added up.

head(cornwall_flows)
       lsoa practice patients
1 E01018750   L82012     2185
2 E01018750   L82016       35
3 E01018750   L82025        1
4 E01018750   L82046        4
5 E01018750   L82066        1
6 E01018751   L82012     1691
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
flows
<spax obs> flows: 3,188 origin-facility counts, total 601,269; loss poisson

flows declares all 3,188 rows, the Isles of Scilly included. The print names the loss, Poisson by default, which is how a fit compares modeled with observed counts. spax() matches the rows to the IDs of the data when it fits a model, and says in a message what it sets aside. The code fits the conditional logit model to the mainland data.

clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
observed: 2,290 counts from 1 origin outside the data or left out by it are dropped; 5 counts at 1 facility outside the data are not fitted (outside = "known" uses them as outside counts)

The 2,290 registrations of residents of the Scilly small area are dropped, because that area is not in the data. The 5 registrations of mainland residents at the Scilly practice are at a practice outside the data, so they belong to the outside option. By default the fit does not know how many of an area’s residents registered outside the data, so it fits only the counts at the 54 practices, and these 5 are left out. Where do residents register? reads the fit and shows when the outside counts can be declared known.

spax() matches the IDs of the observed counts to the data as text. If your codes were read as numbers and lost their leading zeros, it matches each one by its numeric value (1234 to "01234") when exactly one ID of the data has that value, and says so in a message. prep_data() makes no such allowance, so keep IDs as text from the start.
